clue.text: Demanding wicked hair covering in …

indicators.note: covering means laying one thing over another so it takes its place, so the hair word sits where the little word stood

parts.note: wicked means morally bad
a tress is a lock of hair
taken as written: the letters to be covered over

explanation.surface: A wicked hairstyle that covers you up is a demanding look, with the ellipsis carrying the thought into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: TRESS replaces the IN of SINFUL, giving STRESSFUL. The trailing dots join this clue to 6 Across for the surface only.
explanation.definitionFit: A demanding job or day puts you under pressure and strain, which is what stressful describes.

clue.text: Gnome used to be the wrong way round

indicators.note: turned the wrong way round, the word is read backwards

parts.note: 'used to be' puts this in the past tense; the form for 'used' here is was

explanation.surface: A garden ornament that once faced the other direction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gnome' looks like a garden figure; it is the rarer word for a pithy maxim.
explanation.definitionFit: A gnome in this sense is an aphorism or maxim, and an old saying is a saw.

clue.text: Intrigue as Mr Big regularly seen on screen

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: the second and fourth letters
to screen candidates is to vet them

explanation.surface: A crime boss on screen proves fascinating viewing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seen on' places the screen word after the letters in this across-style reading.
explanation.definitionFit: To intrigue someone is to fascinate and hold their attention, as a riveting story does.

clue.text: Almost convinced benefit should support redundant

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the last letter goes

parts.note: sure means convinced
a plus is an advantage or benefit

explanation.surface: A confident view that welfare payments should back those laid off.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue the supporting piece sits underneath. 'Redundant' tempts with its job-loss sense; here it means superfluous.
explanation.definitionFit: Redundant can mean more than needed, and surplus is what is excess to requirements.

clue.text: Foreign Office assuming young, unknown soldier will be highly decorated

indicators.note: assuming means taking on, so the Foreign Office abbreviation takes the young word inside it

parts.note: FO is the Foreign Office, the British department for foreign affairs
a lamb is a young sheep
y is a standard algebraic unknown
a soldier ant is a type of ant

explanation.surface: A Foreign Office posting for a young unknown soldier will bring medals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Highly decorated' suggests medals; here it means ornate and showy.
explanation.definitionFit: Flamboyant is used of ornate, florid styles, as in Flamboyant Gothic architecture with its elaborate tracery.

clue.text: Terms of local area network broken by electronic security breach?

indicators.note: broken by means split open with something forced in between
a term is an end point, so each word gives its final letter

parts.note: the last letter of each of the three words
E is the standard abbreviation for electronic, as in e-mail

explanation.surface: An IT department warning about a breach in the office computer network.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Local area network' is meant to be read as LAN; instead, take the last letter of each word. E goes after the first.
explanation.definitionFit: A leak is the unauthorised disclosure of secrets, a failure of security; the question mark flags the loose fit.

clue.text: … unique hairdressers, maybe with first cut conclusively free

indicators.note: the opening letter of the word for hairdressers is chopped off

parts.note: a salon is a hairdresser's premises; 'maybe' marks it as one example

indicators.note: conclusively points to how a word ends, so only its closing letter is wanted

parts.note: the last letter of free

explanation.surface: Continuing 1 Across: a one-off hair salon, maybe offering a free first cut.
explanation.walkthrough: SALON loses its S, then the E ending free is added.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unique stands by itself with nothing like it, i.e. it is alone in its class.

clue.text: Country album's cover version of I Care

indicators.note: a version is a reworking, so the letters are rearranged
a cover wraps around the outside, so only the outer letters are taken

parts.note: the first and last letters of album
these five letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A country-music album opens with a cover of a song called I Care.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country album' and 'cover version' are both music phrases that come apart: Country is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: America, the United States, is a country.

clue.text: Do too much exercise in obvious downpour

parts.note: overt means open and obvious
a downpour is heavy rain

explanation.surface: Running in an obvious cloudburst is overdoing the workout.
explanation.definitionFit: To overtrain is an athlete's term for exercising beyond what the body can recover from.

clue.text: Enemies rest up after losing independent vote in far from moderate state

indicators.note: up as in stirred up or mixed up, so the letters are thrown into disorder
losing one thing for another here means swapping the independent letter out for the vote mark

parts.note: taken as written
I is the abbreviation for independent
a vote is marked with a cross, X, on a ballot paper

explanation.surface: Political opponents rally after an independent's poll defeat leaves a polarised country.
explanation.walkthrough: X replaces the I of ENEMIES REST, then all eleven letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Extremeness is the quality of being extreme, the opposite of moderation, hence a state far from moderate.

clue.text: Change disclaimer for the audience

indicators.note: an audience listens, so the word is taken by its sound rather than its spelling

parts.note: a waiver is a document giving up a right, a kind of disclaimer

explanation.surface: A broadcaster altering the small-print notice read out to viewers.
explanation.definitionFit: To waver is to shift back and forth, fluctuate or vary, so it is a verb of change.

clue.text: Incredulity as online retailer not working to fix missing copyright

indicators.note: not working is 'not on', so the letters spelling on are removed
missing means lacking, so the abbreviation for copyright is taken out

parts.note: Amazon is the best-known online retailer
to cement is to fix firmly
C (as in the © symbol) stands for copyright

explanation.surface: Shock that an online shop that's down fails to sort out a missing copyright notice.
explanation.walkthrough: AMAZON drops ON (working), and CEMENT drops C (copyright).
explanation.definitionFit: Amazement is astonished disbelief at something surprising, which is close to incredulity.

clue.text: Slowly times boring minutes

indicators.note: something boring drills into whatever surrounds it, so the times word goes inside

parts.note: minute (pronounced my-NEWT) means tiny, and the plural here asks for two of them
times as in multiplication: two by three

explanation.surface: Time crawls when every minute is dull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minutes' wants to be units of time; here it is the adjective minute (tiny) twice over, with BY between.
explanation.definitionFit: Little by little is an idiom for gradually, in small steps, so it means slowly.

clue.text: Politician needs a role with Reform — ultimately by-election should follow

indicators.note: to reform is to form again, so the letters are reshaped

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: ultimately means at the very end, so only the closing letter is used

parts.note: the final letter of by-election

explanation.surface: A politician needs a job with the Reform party, so a by-election must come next.
explanation.walkthrough: Lee Anderson is the MP for Ashfield who defected from the Conservatives to Reform UK in 2024, which the surface alludes to.
explanation.definitionFit: Lee Anderson is a British MP, so he is a politician.

clue.text: See 11
A very quiet organ on a new church show

parts.note: taken as written
pp, pianissimo, is the musical marking for very quiet
the ear is a sense organ
taken as written
N is the abbreviation for new
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A very quiet organ performance at a new church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Organ' summons a church instrument; here it is a body part.
explanation.definitionFit: A show of something is an outward appearance of it, as in a show of strength.

clue.text: Mission involved maybe capturing elite Nazis

indicators.note: capturing means taking prisoner, so the Nazi abbreviation is held inside the other word
involved means tangled or convoluted, so the letters get jumbled up

parts.note: taken as written
the SS was the elite Nazi paramilitary corps

explanation.surface: A wartime operation that may have involved rounding up members of Hitler's SS.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capturing' places SS inside the mixture; all seven letters are then rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A diplomatic mission is the body of envoys sent abroad, housed in an embassy.

clue.text: Implored representative of parliament to get involved with crooked members?

indicators.note: getting involved means getting caught up inside, so the representative goes in

parts.note: implored means begged
a parliament is the collective noun for owls, so one owl represents the group

explanation.surface: Pleading for an MP to be dragged into a scandal with corrupt colleagues.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crooked members' reads as dishonest MPs; members are limbs, here bent legs.
explanation.definitionFit: Bow-legged describes legs that curve outward at the knee, so its limbs are bent.

clue.text: Quiet is helping gripping account

indicators.note: gripping means holding tightly, so the helping word clasps the account abbreviation within

parts.note: a plate (plateful) is a helping of food
AC is the standard abbreviation for account

explanation.surface: A librarian's notice: keeping quiet is a help when you're absorbed in a story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quiet' looks like an adjective but is the verb: to quieten someone down.
explanation.definitionFit: To placate an angry person is to calm or pacify them, i.e. to quiet them.

clue.text: A record peak

parts.note: taken as written
an LP is a long-playing vinyl record

explanation.surface: A sporting best that is a high point.
explanation.definitionFit: An alp is a high mountain, so it is a mountain peak.

clue.text: Modern drag queen finally gets Harlow, for example

parts.note: modern means new
to tow is to drag along

indicators.note: finally points to the very end of a word, so only its closing letter is used

parts.note: the final letter of queen

explanation.surface: A contemporary drag queen ends up in Harlow, an Essex town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drag queen' is a single phrase on the surface, but drag and queen do separate jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: Harlow, in Essex, is one of the planned settlements built in Britain after 1945, officially designated a new town.

clue.text: One who is bound to tell tale about leader of government being overwhelmed by honour

indicators.note: about means around, so the tale word wraps round the letter

parts.note: the OBE is a British honour, Officer of the Order of the British Empire

indicators.note: overwhelmed means engulfed, so the whole lot sits inside the honour

parts.note: to tell a tale is to lie

indicators.note: the leader is the one at the front, so only the first letter is taken

parts.note: the first letter of government

explanation.surface: Someone who must report how a government leader was showered with honours.
explanation.walkthrough: Two layers of nesting: the government letter sits inside the tale, and both sit inside the honour. The OBE is a common crossword honour.
explanation.definitionFit: In law an obligee is a party to an obligation, a person bound up in a bond or contract.

clue.text: Understanding nurses taking temperature the hospital ignored

indicators.note: taking means taking in, so the nurses hold the temperature letter between them

parts.note: EN is an enrolled nurse; two of them for the plural
T is the abbreviation for temperature

indicators.note: something ignored is left out, so the hospital abbreviation drops from the word

parts.note: taken as written
H is the map and sign abbreviation for hospital

explanation.surface: Nurses and doctors agree that taking a temperature can skip the hospital visit.
explanation.walkthrough: EN, an enrolled nurse, is a common crossword abbreviation; the plural 'nurses' supplies two of them, placed either side of the temperature.
explanation.definitionFit: An entente is a friendly agreement between nations, such as the Entente Cordiale, so it is an understanding.

clue.text: Calling bird landing then flying away

parts.note: a tit is a small songbird

indicators.note: something flying away departs, so the word for then leaves the larger word

parts.note: taken as written
and, as in 'and then', means then

explanation.surface: A bird's call as it lands and then takes off again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Calling' looks like a bird's cry; it is the noun sense of naming. The little word 'then' is what flies out of 'landing'.
explanation.definitionFit: Titling something is naming it, and to call someone by a name is likewise to name them.

clue.text: After Chuck Berry's lover settles with the related singers

indicators.note: after being chucked, thrown about, the letters land in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Once Chuck Berry is out of the picture, his lover settles down with the family of singers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chuck Berry' reads as the rock'n'roll star; split them, and Chuck is the mixing signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The Everly Brothers, Don and Phil, were an American rock and roll duo who were siblings, hence related.

clue.text: See 22
Standing back without ceremonial robes

indicators.note: back means read in the opposite direction, from right to left
robes means clothes or wraps, so the following words enfold the answer

parts.note: the letters span the end of without and the start of ceremonial

explanation.surface: A dignitary standing at the back without the robes of office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like the instruction to remove the robes; it is part of the letter string.
explanation.definitionFit: Erect means upright, standing straight up.

clue.text: Complaint as loud buzzer starts

parts.note: a bee is a buzzing insect
f, forte, is the musical marking for loud

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles as a loud alarm goes off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buzzer starts' puts the insect first, ahead of the loudness letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A beef is slang for a grievance or grumble, a complaint.

clue.text: Drop part of course on source of eye colour

parts.note: to sag is to droop or drop

indicators.note: a source is where something starts, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: the first letter of eye
a green is the area of a golf course around the hole

explanation.surface: A golfer's tip: drop your ball on part of the course and keep your eye on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' puts the course part next to the eye letter; 'Eye colour' is a false phrase, since only colour defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Sage green is a soft greyish-green shade, named after the leaves of the herb.

clue.text: Still stored in container terminal

indicators.note: stored in says the letters are kept inside the following words, packed across them

parts.note: the letters run across the end of container and the start of terminal

explanation.surface: Cargo still waiting in a dockside container terminal.
explanation.definitionFit: Inert means motionless or not moving, which is still in its adjective sense.

clue.text: Flatter all but me and Jack

indicators.note: all but means everything except, so the following pronoun is subtracted

parts.note: flatter in its comparative sense: duller, less lively
taken as written

explanation.surface: Praise everyone except me and Jack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flatter' looks like a verb meaning praise; it is the comparative adjective, as in a flatter performance.
explanation.definitionFit: Jack and tar are both old slang words for a sailor.

clue.text: Returning, say, nearly naked to commence jog

indicators.note: nearly means not quite all, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: nude means naked

indicators.note: returning means going back, so the abbreviation is read from the far end

parts.note: e.g. means 'for example', i.e. say

explanation.surface: A streaker coming back, almost undressed, to start a run.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Returning' applies only to 'say'; 'to commence' puts the naked piece at the start even though it comes second in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: To jog someone is to give them a nudge, a little push or prod.

clue.text: Ship's father figure discovered here

parts.note: Fr is the abbreviation for Father, a priest's title
eight is a number, a figure

indicators.note: dis-covered means with its cover taken off, so the outer letters go and the middle stays

parts.note: the middle letters of here

explanation.surface: A ship's paternal figurehead found right here.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Father figure' is a false phrase: the two words give separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A freighter is a cargo vessel, a type of ship.
